meta.title: copilot edited an ad into my pr
meta.author: msanft

comments.author: pushcx
comments.text: An HN comment dates these ads as starting May 2025, and another claims to be from "the Copilot coding agent team" saying they've now disabled the ads.

comments.author: offby1
comments.text: Tim does in fact work for the relevant team.

comments.author: altano
comments.text: No no: they disabled the “tips.”

comments.author: hoistbypetard
comments.text:
Play stupid games, win stupid prizes.

While I’d hope this would dissuade people from turning these things loose on their repos, I rather suspect it won’t change very many minds. And it seems plausible that the only way to avoid “help” from copilot at some point will be to avoid GitHub.

comments.author: telemachus
comments.text:
While I’d hope this would dissuade people from turning these things loose on their repos, I rather suspect it won’t change very many minds.


Over the weekend, I mentioned to my wife that I'm (still) always surprised when I get an email from someone and at the bottom it says "sent from my iPhone." It's not hard to remove that ad, but plenty of people can't be bothered. tl;dr: this is the same thing but in a different context.

comments.author: gerikson
comments.text:
Isn't that basically to excuse an email's brevity?

I've seen similar signatures from Samsung phones, btw.

comments.author: telemachus
comments.text:
Isn't that basically to excuse an email's brevity?


Maybe. I've seen people adapt the signature to say, in some form, "Please excuse any typos or bad grammar. This came from a phone." But the literal "sent from my iPhone" is an ad in my eyes, even if it can excuse brevity or typos as a side-effect.


I've seen similar signatures from Samsung phones, btw.


Sure. I never said it was only iPhones. My larger point remains this: a lot of people don't care about  easily removed ads in their emails (or pull requests), which surprises me.

comments.text: I agree with you, I want to add another ad placement. "Sent from Twitter for iPhone". IMO in this case it's more about status, but even so, it can't be removed.

comments.author: hsivonen
comments.text: It is an ad and a disclaimer. As is Co-authored-by: Claude.

comments.author: sjamaan
comments.text: I've seen someone use "sent from my emacs" in their signature as a joke and snark against those stupid iPhone messages. Thought it was funny.

comments.author: ashwinsundar
comments.text: GitHub has gotten more aggressive about forcing itself into my repos lately.  I notice an "Agents" tab prominently displayed on all my private repos, even though I don't pay for copilot and never remember enabling it.

comments.author: telemachus
comments.text: Several of the newest copilot features are opt-out rather than opt-in. And some of them cannot be turned off at all. That said, if I create a new repository (public or private), I do not see an Agents tab. I recommend you check your copilot settings and turn off everything you can: https://github.com/settings/copilot/features.

comments.author: nemith
comments.text: Even if these are "tips" and not ads in what world is a PR description the best place for such a thing?!?  You own the platform!

comments.author: altano
comments.text: In the world where people stopped looking at your platform’s chrome cause they’re so sick of copilot ads and you’re chasing a place they still look to hit your metrics goals

comments.author: reezer
comments.text: In the same world in which people pay extra money, because "they don't make money with ads" to get a "Sent from my iPhone" tucked onto every message.

comments.author: pscanf
comments.text:
I've been using CodeRabbit for code reviews, and I shouldn't really criticize it since I don't pay a cent for it (OSS plan) and I actually find it super useful. But I'm unreasonably peeved by the default configuration which completely spams your PRs with shit like flow charts that make absolutely no sense (why would a PR need a flow chart?), or even worse cutesy poems about the changes.

I really wonder who finds these things good or in any way useful. It feels like the classic "your scientists were so preoccupied with whether or not they could that they didn't stop to think if they should" situation.

comments.author: viraptor
comments.text:
why would a PR need a flow chart?


Some do, especially when you're reordering some complicated flows, or change infra routing. But it takes skill to know when they're actually interesting.

comments.author: pscanf
comments.text: Yeah, in some cases they can definitely help. Forcing them as default in all cases just produces spam, though, and you either turn them off or tune them out.

comments.author: jonathannen
comments.text:
I know this is tagged vibecoding, but I feel this is the inevitable outcome of an overzealous product team — that said, AI does make this easier to do (?) and the hype machine has put pressure on teams to attempt things like this.

At some stage Microsoft is going to realize they own a social platform in GH and I wonder what that will bring.

comments.author: mcherm
comments.text:
To me, it is very important to know which AI vendors are maintaining a STRICT BRIGHT LINE between the output of the tool and a marketing or advertising.

Marketing or advertising inserted into the AI's output could be incredibly subtle, but it also means there is a fundamental mismatch: the tool is not working for me, it is working for some combination of me and the advertisers.

If one AI company understands how important this is and makes a big deal out of making certain that no advertising ever affects the output of the tool, and another AI company experiments with what level of intrusiveness they can get away with without losing customers, then I want to work only with the first company, not the second.

comments.author: sjamaan
comments.text: Oh man, I just got nightmare visions of vibecoded PRs which insert ads into the code's comments...

comments.author: jonathannen
comments.text:
"Bright line" might be hard to achieve (I'm not glad of the fact). And I don't think it's stable. "Ad" vs "tip" vs "useful" is extremely subjective -- not in this case I know, but it's definitely a continuum.

Not only is it outright subjective, I think there is a generational shift too.

comments.author: mcherm
comments.text:
I think you are totally right about the ambiguity. But I also can see a difference between some vendors who are trying to draw a bright line[1] (even if they might not draw it in the perfect spot), and others who are experimenting to see where they can place it. [2]

[1] https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-is-a-space-to-think

[2] https://notes.zachmanson.com/copilot-edited-an-ad-into-my-pr/
